name: Bronze Age steppe peoples
summary: Herders of the Eurasian steppe such as the Yamnaya, Afanasievo, Catacomb, Andronovo and Karasuk cultures, who used wagons and later chariots. Many scholars link them to the spread of Indo-European languages.

knownFor.label: Spoked-wheel chariot
knownFor.note: Light chariots found in Sintashta graves, among the earliest.

knownFor.label: Kurgan burials
knownFor.note: Burial mounds over graves of important people.

knownFor.label: Horse riding
knownFor.note: Horses became central to steppe life.

location.value: Andronovo culture: the southern Urals to the upper Yenisei and western Xinjiang, with sites in Kazakhstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan (not Ukraine).

urbanisation.value: Villages of about two to twenty houses, some up to a hundred; Sintashta (c. 2200–1900 BC) is now thought distinct from Andronovo.

disease.value: A Yersinia pestis strain from the Kytmanovo site (1746–1626 BC) has been studied; the article says it was “not the plague”.

migration.value: Steppe peoples moved into Europe and Asia; their genes are found widely.
migration.source: Wikipedia: Yamnaya culture; Wikipedia: Andronovo culture

economicBase.value: Herding cattle, sheep and horses; some farming.

religion.value: A ritual “head and hooves” horse burial cult; burials with livestock, wheeled vehicles and horse cheek-pieces.

languageWriting.value: Most researchers associate Andronovo with early Indo-Iranian languages; the link is debated (the lead calls it agreed).

artsArchitecture.value: Kurgans with timber or stone chambers; copper-working workshops.

neighbours.value: Farming peoples of Europe, Central Asia and China.

ideasReligions.value: The Indo-Iranian link is debated: Klejn and Brentjes argue the culture is too late for it.

colonisation.value: Moved into Europe, Iran and India (debated).

peakPeriod.value: Andronovo culture, c. 2000–1150 BC (per the infobox; the first stage may have begun in the late 3rd millennium BC).

outcome.value: Karasuk succeeded Andronovo in southern Siberia and Kazakhstan (1500–800 BC); Iranian-speaking nomads (Saka, Sarmatians, Alans) dominated the 1st millennium BC.
